blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 31 (Materials and Energy), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define a material. On what are materials understood and selected? Name five classes of materials discussed in the chapter with one use of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Material: any substance or mixture of substances that makes up a physical object of daily-life or industrial importance, e.g. plastics, metals, ceramics, building material.

Understanding: materials have superior thermal, mechanical (hardness, elasticity) and chemical properties; they are understood by their composition, the nature of their chemical bonds and their microstructure.

Selection: a material is chosen for an application depending on its physical, chemical, mechanical, electrical and thermal characteristics.

Classes and uses:
• Metals and alloys – steel in bridges, copper in electric wires
• Ceramics – refractory bricks, porcelain insulators, spark plugs (alumina)
• Polymers – large organic or inorganic molecules, e.g. poly(ethene) bags
• Composites – fibreglass boat hulls and car bodies
• Semiconductors – silicon in microchips and solar panels

book_ref.quote: Materials have superior thermal, mechanical (e.g., hardness, elasticity, etc.) and chemical properties.

blocks.prompt: 2 Describe the properties of metals and how they occur in nature. Explain ores and gangue with an example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Properties: metals are hard, rigid substances and good conductors of heat and electricity. They are malleable and ductile, so they can be rolled into sheets or drawn into wires without fracture. Steel is used in bridges (strength), aluminium in aircraft bodies (light weight) and copper in electric wires (conductivity).

Occurrence: metals are mostly found in the earth's crust.
• Free state: less reactive metals such as gold and platinum exist in the metallic state and rarely form compounds.
• Combined state: more reactive metals such as sodium, aluminium, iron and copper exist as ores, e.g. haematite (Fe₂O₃) is an ore of iron.

Ores and gangue: ores are not pure compounds but mixtures of the desired metal compound, impurities and earthly materials; the earthly materials are called gangue. Metals are extracted from ores by a series of physical and chemical processes (metallurgy).

book_ref.quote: Metals are mostly found in the earth crust.

blocks.prompt: 3 Explain the conversion of a concentrated ore into the metal oxide. Describe roasting and calcination with equations and compare them. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
After mining and ore concentration, the concentrated ore is converted into the metal oxide, mostly in two ways.

Roasting: a sulphide ore of the metal is heated with an excess supply of air.
2ZnS(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2ZnO(s) + 2SO₂(g)

Calcination: a metal carbonate ore is heated in a limited or no air environment to convert it into its oxide.
ZnCO₃(s) → ZnO(s) + CO₂(g)

The oxide is then reduced to the metal.

book_ref.quote: Metallurgy involves a series of processes to finally obtain the purest form of a metal.

blocks.prompt: 4 Describe the reduction of metal oxides to metals. Explain the carbon (CO) method and the electrolytic method, giving the metals for which each is used. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Reduction of metal oxides is the most important step of metal extraction; the technique depends on the reactivity of the metal.

(i) Reduction with carbon: used for less reactive metals (below carbon in the reactivity series). Carbon is first converted into CO, which displaces oxygen from the metal oxide to form the free metal. Iron ore:
C + ½O₂ → CO
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂

(ii) Electrolytic method: carbon cannot reduce oxides of metals more reactive than carbon. Their compounds are melted and an electric current is passed, which requires significant energy. The positive metal ions move to the negative electrode (cathode), where they gain electrons to form the metal.
Used for highly reactive metals such as Na, K and Al, and for achieving very high purity in less reactive metals such as Cu.

book_ref.quote: Different techniques are used for different metals depending on their reactivity.

blocks.prompt: 5 388 g of zinc sulphide is roasted: 2ZnS(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2ZnO(s) + 2SO₂(g). Calculate (i) the mass of oxygen used, (ii) the mass of ZnO formed and (iii) the mass of SO₂ released. (Molar masses: ZnS = 97, O₂ = 32, ZnO = 81, SO₂ = 64 g mol⁻¹.) Show that mass is conserved. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Change grams of ZnS to moles, use the 2 : 3 : 2 : 2 mole ratio, then change moles back to grams.

book_ref.quote: This can be done in two ways, mostly.

blocks.final_answer: O₂ used = 192 g; ZnO = 324 g; SO₂ = 256 g; total mass 580 g on both sides.

blocks.prompt: 6 480 kg of haematite (Fe₂O₃) is reduced: C + ½O₂ → CO and Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate (i) the moles of CO needed, (ii) the mass of carbon needed to make this CO and (iii) the mass of iron produced. (Molar masses: Fe₂O₃ = 160, C = 12, Fe = 56 g mol⁻¹.) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find kmol of Fe₂O₃; each needs 3 CO (one C per CO) and gives 2 Fe.

book_ref.quote: An example is the reduction of the iron ore as follows:

steps: Moles of Fe₂O₃ = 480 000 g / 160 = 3000 mol = 3.0 kmol
C needed = 9.0 kmol (1 C → 1 CO) → 9.0 × 12 = 108 kg
blocks.final_answer: CO = 9.0 kmol; carbon = 108 kg; iron = 336 kg.

blocks.prompt: 7 What is alloying and why is it done? Give the constituents, properties and uses of four common alloys. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Alloying is the mixing of two or more metals to give a homogeneous solution, or the mixing of a metal with a non-metal. It is done to alter the microstructure of the metal so as to enhance properties such as strength, corrosion resistance and electrical or magnetic properties. It is the last step of metallurgy, after refining.

book_ref.quote: Alloying involves the mixing of any two or more metals to give a homogeneous solution

rows: Iron (98-99%) + carbon (0.1-2%) (and Cr, Ni, Mn, Si, S)

blocks.prompt: 8 What are ceramics? Give their chemical nature and explain their important properties with an application of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Ceramics are hard but brittle materials with high melting temperatures and very good insulating capabilities, which fit them for high-temperature and electrical applications.

Chemical nature: a blend of silicates and oxides of alkali and alkaline earth metals and aluminium, such as K₂O, Na₂O, CaO, Al₂SiO₅. Their strong bonds and fixed structures give strength, durability and resistance to corrosion and heat.

Uses: pottery, furnaces, tiles and sanitary ware (porcelain), windows and optical fibres (glass), spark plugs (alumina).

book_ref.quote: which make them fit in high temperature and electrical applications

rows: High melting point – remain solid at very high temperatures
Hardness and wear resistance – extremely difficult to scratch
Abrasives (silicon carbide in sandpaper), cutting tools
Electrical insulator – most do not conduct electricity
Chemical inertness – resist corrosion and chemical attack
Ceramic coatings on chemical processing equipment

blocks.prompt: 9 What is a composite? Describe fibreglass and carbon fibre as composites, giving their properties and uses. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A composite is a combination of two or more materials forming a product with better properties. It has a matrix and one or more reinforcement agents caged in the matrix.

Fibreglass: a polymer forms the matrix; the reinforcement may be fibres of a fabric, glass or carbon-based materials. Uses: boat hulls and car bodies; insulating walls and ceilings from heat and cold (Figure 31.3).

Carbon fibre: widely used in the aircraft and sports-gear industry because of its lightness and strong durability.

Properties of composites: good strength-to-weight ratio and strong resistance to corrosion, so they suit demanding applications.

book_ref.quote: Composites are very efficient and useful modern day materials.

blocks.prompt: 10 What are semiconductors? How do they differ from conductors? Describe silicon, gallium arsenide and gallium nitride with their applications. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Semiconductors are substances that conduct electricity only in special conditions and are sensitive to light, heat and voltage, which makes them important in modern electronics.

Difference from conductors: the current passing through a semiconductor can be controlled as demanded in an application.

• Silicon (Si): the most common semiconductor, highly effective and abundant; used in microchips and solar panels. A mobile SIM card is a silicon chip with minor parts such as copper connectors; silicon can conduct, store and process data in a device.
• Gallium arsenide (GaAs): used in wireless communication, e.g. 5G internet devices.
• Gallium nitride (GaN): used in electric cars for fast charging due to its advanced conductivity.

book_ref.quote: Due to these characteristics, they are important in modern electronic applications.

blocks.prompt: 11 Define toxicity. Explain the health, physical and environmental hazards of materials with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Toxicity is the extent to which a substance can harm an organism or the environment. A material may be toxic during its production, use and final disposal; toxicity is measured by the extent and type of hazard it may cause.

(i) Health hazards: a substance damages health on exposure. Metals like chromium are carcinogens (cause cancer), mutagens (change DNA and genes) and cause respiratory issues; some additives in plastics cause hormonal problems.

(ii) Physical hazards: due to physical or chemical properties, harm may happen to buildings, humans, ecosystems and the environment, e.g. a flammable or explosive material can harm humans, forests or a building.

(iii) Environmental hazards: substances cause long-term harm to aquatic life or the environment. Heavy metals like lead, mercury and cadmium leach into soil and groundwater and are dangerous to plants, land animals, fish and other aquatic organisms.

book_ref.quote: Hazards posed by a material are of many types.

blocks.prompt: 12 Discuss heavy metals and plastics as major toxic materials. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Plastics and heavy metals are two major concerns. They are commonly used because of their superior properties, but their long-term effects are lethal.

Heavy metals: lead (Pb), mercury (Hg) and cadmium (Cd) are common in electronics, batteries and fluorescent lights. They can get into groundwater, from where they transfer to living organisms.

Plastics: many plastics contain toxic additives such as phthalates or bisphenol A (BPA), which can interfere with hormones. Microplastics are now found in oceans, soil and even food, with long-term effects on human lives and ecosystems.

book_ref.quote: These materials are commonly used due to their superior properties.

blocks.prompt: 13 Explain the importance of recycling and describe the three main challenges associated with it. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Importance: recycling is an important part of waste management, conservation of resources and energy saving. It minimizes solid waste in landfills, preserves limited natural resources such as metals, oil and timber, and saves energy – recycling aluminium consumes 95 percent less energy than recovering it from the raw ore.

Challenges:
(i) Material separation: most present-day products (mobile phones, laptops) are made of mixed materials that are not easily separated, e.g. plastic coating on metals or multi-layered packaging films.
(ii) Expensive reprocessing: sorting, cleaning and other steps are expensive, and reprocessing plastics and electronics needs a lot of energy; this is uneconomical when the materials are available elsewhere at a lower price.
(iii) Contamination: recycled metals and plastics can be contaminated by dyes, chemicals or biological materials, decreasing quality and safety; contaminated plastic cannot be recycled for food-grade use.

book_ref.quote: Recycling is an important aspect of waste management, conservation of resources and energy saving.

blocks.prompt: 14 Describe the methods and chemical principles of recycling plastics, metals, paper and glass. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Table 31.3 summarises how important materials are recycled.

book_ref.quote: Table 31.3 Principles and methods of recycling of some important materials

rows: Sorting, cleaning, melting and reforming the plastic; limited by contamination and degradation of polymer chains
Breaking polymer chains into the original monomers or simpler chemicals using heat, solvents or catalysts; produces purer reactants
Metals (steel, aluminium) – thermal and chemical refining (metallurgy)
Melting and refining to remove impurities; requires significant energy, but much less than primary production
Chemical and mechanical separation of fibres; pulp treated with NaOH or Na₂CO₃ to remove inks and dyes
Cleaning, crushing and melting scrap glass (cullet) to form new glass; chemically simpler as glass is a non-crystalline solid

blocks.prompt: 15 A plant recycles 2.5 tonnes (2500 kg) of aluminium. If producing 1 kg of aluminium from its raw ore needs 200 MJ (assumed value), calculate (i) the energy needed to produce this aluminium from ore, (ii) the energy needed to recycle it, and (iii) the energy saved. Use the chapter's figure for the saving. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Recycling aluminium uses 95% less energy, i.e. only 5% of the primary energy.

book_ref.quote: the recycling of aluminium consumes 95 percent less energy

steps: Energy saved = 500 000 − 25 000 = 475 000 MJ (= 95% of the primary energy)
blocks.final_answer: From ore: 5.0 × 10⁵ MJ; recycling: 2.5 × 10⁴ MJ; saved: 4.75 × 10⁵ MJ.

blocks.prompt: 16 Write a note on X-ray crystallography: what it is, why X-rays are used, and its applications in science and industry. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
X-ray crystallography is a very strong analytical tool used to identify the three-dimensional positions of atoms in a crystalline solid. It is important in material science, biochemistry and pharmaceutical chemistry because it lets scientists visualize material structures.

Why X-rays: X-rays have a very small wavelength, so this electromagnetic radiation can find the positions of electrons and atoms in a molecule or ionic compound. Solids consist of layers or strands of atoms; X-rays falling on a crystal are diffracted at specific angles and the diffracted rays make diffraction patterns on a screen. Analysed with mathematical models, the pattern gives a map of atomic positions, bond angles and electron density (e.g. naphthalene, Figure 31.5).

Applications:
• Determination of the double helix structure of DNA (its best-known use)
• Analysing complex biomolecules such as enzymes and proteins
• Pharmaceutical drug development – seeing how a drug molecule attaches to its target
• Analysis of minerals, synthetic crystals and nanomaterials, to enhance material performance in electronics, optics and construction

book_ref.quote: It is important in material science, biochemistry, and pharmaceutical chemistry

blocks.prompt: 17 What are fossil fuels? Describe petroleum, natural gas and coal with their main products and uses, and state the environmental effect of burning them. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Petroleum (crude oil), coal and natural gas are collectively called fossil fuels.

Petroleum: mined from underground reservoirs and refined in large plants by fractional distillation. Major products: naphtha, gasoline, kerosene and diesel. Uses: transportation fuels (petrol, diesel) and lubricants.

Natural gas: mainly methane (CH₄) mixed with ethane, propane and butane. Methane is used to produce ammonia (fertilizers) and methanol (solvents and fuel). Uses: cooking, heating, electricity and fertilizer production.

Coal: less useful than before but still a petrochemical raw material where reserves are high; it gives benzene, toluene and xylene for dyes, resins and explosives. Uses: electricity generation, cement and steel industries.

Environmental effect: although highly efficient, burning fossil fuels produces greenhouse gases such as CO₂, leading to air pollution, global warming and climate change.

book_ref.quote: Crude oil is mined at the underground reservoirs and refined in large size plants

blocks.prompt: 18 Describe the fractional distillation of crude oil. Name its fractions with their temperature ranges and uses. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Crude oil is a complicated mixture of hydrocarbons. Fractional distillation separates it physically on the basis of the difference in boiling points of the hydrocarbons.

Process: the crude oil is heated in a furnace until it vaporizes. The vapour passes into a fractionating column, a tall tower in which the temperature drops slowly going up. As the vapour rises, constituents condense at different heights according to their boiling points: heavier hydrocarbons with higher boiling points condense near the bottom, lighter ones with low boiling points rise further. The fractions are drawn off at different levels.

Fractional distillation is important because it provides petrochemicals for industrial, domestic and transport use.

book_ref.quote: During this process, the crude oil is heated inside a furnace until it is vaporized.

rows: Gasoline / petrol (up to about 200 °C; e.g. C₈H₁₈)

blocks.prompt: 19 What are petrochemicals and their derivatives? Give six petrochemicals with their derived products and uses. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Petrochemicals are chemicals obtained primarily from crude oil and natural gas by refining and transformation. They are used to make daily items in packaging, construction, textile, electronics and medical sectors.

Derivatives of petrochemicals are synthetic chemicals manufactured from petrochemicals by chemical transformations such as polymerization, oxidation or substitution; they are very important industrial products.

book_ref.quote: They are used to make diverse daily items found in several industries

blocks.prompt: 20 What is cracking and why is it necessary? Describe thermal cracking and catalytic cracking with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Cracking is a chemical process involving the thermal dissociation of large hydrocarbon molecules (typically naphtha or heavy oils) into smaller, more useful molecules such as alkenes. It is necessary because the smaller ethene and propene are the major raw materials for plastics and artificial rubber.

(i) Thermal cracking: very high temperatures (usually 450 °C - 750 °C) and high pressure physically break the C–C bonds. No catalyst is used, so a high energy input is needed. It gives a high percentage of alkenes, important for the plastic industry. Example – decane gives octane and ethene:
C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄

(ii) Catalytic cracking: more efficient and more common in modern refineries. A catalyst, usually zeolites (aluminosilicates) or silica-alumina, significantly lowers the activation energy, so the reaction occurs at a reduced temperature (about 500 °C) and pressure, saving energy and giving better control over products. Example – heavy naphtha gives short-chain alkenes:
Naphtha (heavy hydrocarbons) →(catalyst) C₂H₄ (ethene) + C₃H₆ (propene)

book_ref.quote: There are two primary methods used to achieve this: Thermal Cracking and Catalytic Cracking.

blocks.prompt: 21 What is reforming? State its purpose and explain its three reactions with equations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Reforming is a refining process that rearranges the molecular structure of hydrocarbons. In contrast to cracking (where molecules are broken down), it rearranges straight-chain alkanes into branched or cyclic (aromatic) structures.

Purpose: to enhance fuel quality by converting low-octane straight chains into high-octane branched or aromatic fuels, to avoid engine knocking.

1. Isomerisation (branched hydrocarbons): straight chains become branched-chain isomers of higher octane number.
C₆H₁₄ → iso-C₆H₁₄ (n-hexane to iso-hexane)

2. Cyclization (cyclic hydrocarbons): straight chains are converted into cyclic compounds.
C₆H₁₄ → C₆H₁₂ + H₂ (hexane to cyclohexane)

3. Aromatisation (dehydrocyclisation; printed in the book as dehydrocoupling): hydrogen is lost to give aromatic hydrocarbons such as BTX (benzene, toluene, xylene), the building blocks of plastics, dyes and synthetic fibres. Hexane forms a stable aromatic ring and releases hydrogen as a valuable by-product.
C₆H₁₄ →(Pt catalyst/heat) C₆H₆ + 4H₂ (hexane to benzene)

book_ref.quote: Reforming is a refining process that rearranges the molecular structure of hydrocarbons.

blocks.prompt: 22 Answer both parts. (i) 568 g of decane is thermally cracked: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄. Calculate the masses of octane and ethene formed. (ii) 172 g of hexane is converted into benzene: C₆H₁₄ → C₆H₆ + 4H₂. Calculate the masses of benzene and hydrogen formed. (Molar masses: C₁₀H₂₂ = 142, C₈H₁₈ = 114, C₂H₄ = 28, C₆H₁₄ = 86, C₆H₆ = 78, H₂ = 2 g mol⁻¹.) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Convert the reactant mass to moles, use the mole ratios of each equation, and check that total mass is conserved.

book_ref.quote: can be thermally cracked to produce octane and ethene

blocks.final_answer: (i) Octane 456 g, ethene 112 g; (ii) benzene 156 g, hydrogen 16 g.

blocks.prompt: 23 Define energy density and specific energy. Explain where each is important, with examples of diesel, gasoline, hydrogen and CNG. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Two key aspects are used to evaluate a fuel for an application.

Energy density: the energy capacity of a substance, expressed as the quantity of energy stored per unit volume of a fuel, typically in MJ/L. High-energy-density fuels store large energy in a small volume and are useful in stationary applications and storage, e.g. power plants and generators. Diesel (~35.8 MJ/L) is more energy dense than gasoline (~34.2 MJ/L), i.e. it contains more energy per litre.

Specific energy: the amount of energy contained in a mass, typically in MJ/kg. It matters where weight is critical, as in aviation or spacecraft; a high-specific-energy fuel gives much energy without adding much mass. Hydrogen has an extremely high specific energy (120 MJ/kg), which makes it interesting for aerospace, although its energy density is low.

CNG: economical for transport in Pakistan, but its lower energy density means vehicles must carry more storage volume than for petrol; so it suits local commuting, not long travel.

book_ref.quote: there are two key aspects used to evaluate a fuel

blocks.prompt: 24 A vehicle tank holds 40 L. Using the chapter's values (diesel ~35.8 MJ/L, gasoline ~34.2 MJ/L, hydrogen 120 MJ/kg), calculate (i) the energy in a full tank of diesel and of gasoline, (ii) the extra energy carried by diesel, and (iii) the mass of hydrogen that would carry the same energy as the full diesel tank. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Energy = volume × energy density; mass of hydrogen = energy ÷ specific energy.

book_ref.quote: diesel is more energy dense (~35.8 MJ/L) in comparison to gasoline (~34.2 MJ/L)

blocks.final_answer: Diesel 1432 MJ, gasoline 1368 MJ; diesel carries 64 MJ more; about 11.9 kg of hydrogen carries the same energy.

blocks.prompt: 25 What is nuclear energy? Explain nuclear fission with an equation and the chain reaction, and discuss its use and drawbacks in power generation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Nuclear energy is the energy released by the nuclei of atoms, either when heavy nuclei are split (fission) or when light nuclei are combined (fusion). These reactions liberate extremely high quantities of energy compared with chemical reactions.

Fission: a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239 is split into two lighter nuclei, producing energy, neutrons and radiation.
²³⁵U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3¹₀n + energy

Chain reaction: the neutrons produced can cause additional fission of other nuclei, so the reaction continues by itself.

Use: nuclear power plants extensively use fission to produce electricity; it gives very high energy from small quantities of fuel.

Drawbacks: it produces radioactive waste that must be handled with care over a long duration, and there is a danger of nuclear accidents, e.g. Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011), which seriously harmed the environment and human health (more than 150,000 people were evacuated at Fukushima).

book_ref.quote: Fission is the process in which a heavy atomic nuclei like uranium-235 or plutonium-239 is split

blocks.prompt: 26 Describe the working of a solar photovoltaic (PV) system and state the advantages of solar energy. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A solar PV system is a clean energy system.

Working (Figure 31.7):
• Solar panels, typically of silicon semiconducting materials, convert sunlight into electricity by the photovoltaic effect: exposure to light activates electrons in the material, producing direct current (DC) electricity.
• An inverter converts the DC into alternating current (AC) to power homes, schools, offices and industries.
• Batteries store electricity for use at night or on cloudy days, and also help stabilize voltage and produce surge current.
• Electrical accessories, wires, appliances and mounting structures make the whole system effective and safe.

Advantages:
• Environmentally friendly and renewable, so it helps fight climate change and pollution.
• Cost-effective in the long run, as panels need limited maintenance once installed.
Energy shortages, high fuel prices and climate problems show the need to switch to renewable sources like solar, hydro and wind energy.

book_ref.quote: The exposure of the solar panel activates electrons in the material
